The **Nobel Prize in Literature**, here meaning _for_ Literature (Swedish: _Nobelpriset i litteratur_), is a Swedish literature prize that is awarded annually to an author from any country who has, in the words of Alfred Nobel, "in the field of literature, produced the most outstanding work in an idealistic direction".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelorglit-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-swedishref-3) Though individual works are sometimes cited as being particularly noteworthy, the award is based on an author's body of work as a whole. The Swedish Academy decides who, if anyone, will receive the prize.
The academy announces the name of the laureate in early October. It is one of the five Nobel Prizes established by the will of Alfred Nobel in 1895. Literature is traditionally the final award presented at the Nobel Prize ceremony. On some occasions, the award has been postponed to the following year, most recently in 2018.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelBBC-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-akademi2018-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-krisen-6)

In 1901, French poet and essayist Sully Prudhomme (1839–1907) was the first person to be awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, "in special recognition of his poetic composition, which gives evidence of lofty idealism, artistic perfection, and a rare combination of the qualities of both heart and intellect."
Hemingway's telegram in 1954 (The academy has alternately used _for_ Literature and _in_ Literature over the years, the latter becoming the norm today.)

Alfred Nobel stipulated in his last will and testament that his money be used to create a series of prizes for those who confer the "greatest benefit on mankind" in physics, chemistry, peace, physiology or medicine, and literature.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-BBCHistory-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Britannica6-8) Although Nobel wrote several wills during his lifetime, the last was written a little over a year before he died, and it was signed at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris on 27 November 1895.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-10) Nobel bequeathed 94% of his total assets, 31 million Swedish _kronor_ (US$198 million, €176 million in 2016), to establish and endow the five Nobel Prizes.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Nobelwill-11) Due to the level of scepticism surrounding the will, it was not until 26 April 1897 that the Storting (Norwegian Parliament) approved it.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelprize1-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Levinovitz13-13) The executors of his will were Ragnar Sohlman and Rudolf Lilljequist, who formed the Nobel Foundation to take care of Nobel's fortune and organise the prizes.

The members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee that were to award the Peace Prize were appointed shortly after the will was approved. The prize-awarding organisations followed: the Karolinska Institutet on 7 June, the Swedish Academy on 9 June, and the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences on 11 June.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-15) The Nobel Foundation then reached an agreement on guidelines for how the Nobel Prize should be awarded. In 1900, the Nobel Foundation's newly created statutes were promulgated by King Oscar II.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Levinovitz13-13)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-thelocal1-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-BritannicaWill-17) According to Nobel's will, the prize in literature should be determined by "the Academy in Stockholm", which was specified by the statutes of the Nobel Foundation to mean the Swedish Academy.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Espmark-18)

## Nomination and award procedure
[edit]
Each year, the Swedish Academy sends out requests for nominations of candidates for the Nobel Prize in Literature. Members of the Academy, members of literature academies and societies, professors of literature and language, former Nobel literature laureates, and the presidents of writers' organisations are all allowed to nominate a candidate. One cannot nominate oneself.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobnoma-19)
Between 1901 and 1950, around 20 to 35 nominations were usually received each year.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-20) Since then, thousands of requests are sent out each year, and as of 2011 about 220 proposals were returned.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-wastberg-21) These proposals must be received by the Academy by 1 February, after which they are examined by the Nobel Committee, a working group within the Academy comprising four to five members.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobnomb-22) By April, the committee narrows the field to around 20 candidates.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-wastberg-21) By May, a shortlist of five names is approved by the Academy.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-wastberg-21) The next four months are spent reading and reviewing the works of the five candidates.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-wastberg-21) In October, members of the Academy vote, and the candidate who receives more than half of the votes is named the Nobel laureate in Literature.

## Nomination and award procedure
No one can get the prize without being on the shortlist at least twice; thus, many authors reappear and are reviewed repeatedly over the years.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-wastberg-21) The academicians read works in their original language, but when a candidate is shortlisted from a language that no member masters, they call on translators and oath-sworn experts to provide samples of that writer's work.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-wastberg-21) Other elements of the process are similar to those of other Nobel Prizes.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobnomb-22) The Swedish Academy is composed of 18 members who are elected for life and, until 2018, not technically permitted to leave.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-keyton-23) On 2 May 2018, King Carl XVI Gustaf amended the rules of the academy and made it possible for members to resign. The new rules also mention that a member who has been inactive in the work of the academy for more than two years can be asked to resign.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-DN-April-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-aftonbladetApril-25) The members of the Nobel committee are elected for a period of three years from among the members of the academy and are assisted by specially appointed expert advisers.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-26)

## Nomination and award procedure
The award is usually announced in October. Sometimes, however, the award has been announced the year after the nominal year, the latest such case being the 2018 award. In the midst of controversy surrounding claims of sexual assault, conflict of interest, and resignations by officials, on 4 May 2018, the Swedish Academy announced that the 2018 laureate would be announced in 2019 along with the 2019 laureate.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-akademi2018-5)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelBBC-4) Some years, such as in 1949, no candidate received the required majority of the votes, and for that reason, the prize was postponed and announced the following year.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-27)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Withdrawn, invalidated and unarchived nominations
[edit]
Between 1901 and 1970, literary historians and archivists noted that there were official nominees who were either withdrawn, invalidated or not archived in the Academy's nomination database.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-fact-28) In 1911, the Swedish playwright August Strindberg was nominated for the first time by Academy member Nathan Söderblom but because the nomination "arrived too late", it was withdrawn and unarchived unlike any other nominations that were moved to the succeeding year.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-fact-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-29) In 1904, José Echegaray's nomination letter "arrived late due to slow mail service" and Rudyard Kipling's had been temporarily misplaced. It was then decided by the Nobel committee to include both the nominations for 1904 and not moved for 1905.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-30)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Withdrawn, invalidated and unarchived nominations
There have been nine recorded occasions when the nominations were declared invalid. The only nominations for Pedro Pablo Figueroa, [Max Haushofer Jr.](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max%20Haushofer%20Jr. "de:Max Haushofer Jr."), William Booth and Armando Alvares Pedroso were declared invalid by the Nobel committee because their respective nominators were found to be ineligible.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelpris-32) Such declarations also occurred to Ernest Lavisse in 1911, Henriette Charasson in 1945, Teixeira de Pascoaes in 1945 and Enrique Larreta in 1945._[why?_] Therefore, their names were withdrawn from the archives in those specific years.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelpris-32)John Macmillan Brown's self-nomination under the pseudonym "Godfrey Sweven" was declared invalid due to the rule that nominations of oneself is impermissible.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-33)
Permanent Secretary of the Swedish Academy Anders Österling revealed to the _New York Times_ days before the announcement that Willa Cather, together with Ernest Hemingway, John Steinbeck, and Gabriela Mistral, was among the contenders for the 1944 prize. Despite the revelation, Cather's name was not included in the archives.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-DlN-34)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-35) The prize was eventually given to Johannes V. Jensen.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-DlN-34)
Spanish philologist Ramón Menéndez Pidal was never awarded despite the numerous nominations.

## Nomination and award procedure
### Withdrawn, invalidated and unarchived nominations
With the annual revelation of nominated writers for the Nobel Prize in Literature, interesting facts are eventually uncovered between 1901 and 1975 such as the following:[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-36)
*   **Most nominations in a year**: 205 nominations were made in 1973.  
*   **Most nominations for a nominee**: Spanish philologist Ramón Menéndez Pidal received 92 nominations in 1956.  
*   **Total number of nominees**: 881  
*   **Highest number of nominees in a year**: 114 writers were nominated in 1975.  
*   **Highest number of new nominees in a year:** 30 new writers were nominated in 1969.  
*   **Literary societies**: The Pali Text Society was nominated in 1916 and remains the only society.  
*   **Number of women**: 89  
*   **Most women nominees in a year**: 13 women were nominated in 1975.  
*   **Oldest male nominee**: At age 99, Spanish philologist Ramón Menéndez Pidal was nominated in 1968.  
*   **Oldest female nominee**: At age 92, Estonian poet Marie Under was nominated in 1975.  
*   **Youngest male nominee**: At age 29, Icelandic writer Gunnar Gunnarsson was nominated in 1918.  
*   **Youngest female nominee**: At age 31, Finnish writer Sally Salminen was nominated in 1937.

A Literature Nobel Prize laureate receives a gold medal, a diploma bearing a citation, and a sum of money.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-50) The amount of money awarded depends on the income of the Nobel Foundation that year.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelprize2-51)
The literature prize can be shared between two, but not three, laureates.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-52) If a prize is awarded jointly, the prize money is split equally between them.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-BritannicaPrizes-53)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Withdrawn, invalidated and unarchived nominations
The prize money of the Nobel Prize has been fluctuating since its inauguration but as of 2026 it stood at kr11,000,000 (about US$1,150,000); previously it was kr 10,000,000.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-54)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-prizemoneyref-55)[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-prizemoneyrefpdf-56)
This was not the first time the prize amount was decreased—beginning with a nominal value of kr 150,782 in 1901 (worth 8,123,951 in 2011 SKr) the nominal value has been as low as kr 121,333 (2,370,660 in 2011 SKr) in 1945—but it has been uphill or stable since then, peaking at an SKr-2011 value of 11,659,016 in 2001.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-prizemoneyrefpdf-56)
The laureate is also invited to give a lecture during "Nobel Week" in Stockholm; the highlight is the prize-giving ceremony and banquet on 10 December.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-lectureref-57) It is the third [richest literary prize in the world](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_world's_richest_literary_prizes "List of the world's richest literary prizes").
The literature medal features a portrait of Alfred Nobel in left profile on the obverse.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-NobelUnique-58)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Withdrawn, invalidated and unarchived nominations
It was designed by Erik Lindberg.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-NobelUnique-58) The reverse of the medal depicts a 'young man sitting under a laurel tree who, enchanted, listens to and writes down the song of the Muse'.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-NobelLit-59)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-NobelUnique-58) It is inscribed "_Inventas vitam iuvat excoluisse per artes_" ("It is beneficial to have improved (human) life through discovered arts"), an adaptation of "_inventas aut qui vitam excoluere per artes_" from line 663 of book 6 of the _Aeneid_ by the Roman poet Virgil.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-NobelLit-59) A plate below the figures is inscribed with the name of the recipient. The text "ACAD. SUEC." denoting the Swedish Academy is also inscribed on the reverse.[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-NobelLit-59)
Between 1902 and 2010, the Nobel Prize medals were struck by the Myntverket, the Swedish royal mint, located in Eskilstuna. In 2011, the medals were made by the Det Norske Myntverket in Kongsberg. The medals have been made by Svenska Medalj in Eskilstuna since 2012.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-NobelUnique-58)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Potential candidates
Former recipients of the Nobel Prize in Literature are allowed to nominate their candidates for the prize and sometimes their proposals have subsequently been awarded the prize. The 1912 laureate Gerhart Hauptmann nominated Verner von Heidenstam (awarded in 1916) and Thomas Mann (awarded in 1929), the 1915 laureate Romain Rolland proposed Ivan Bunin (awarded in 1933), Thomas Mann nominated Hermann Hesse (awarded in 1946) in 1931, the 1951 laureate Pär Lagerkvist was proposed by both André Gide and Roger Martin du Gard, and the 1960 laureate Saint-John Perse was nominated several times by the 1948 laureate T. S. Eliot.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-67)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-68)[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-69)
The Swedish Academy's permanent secretary Peter Englund at the announcement of the 2010 Nobel Prize in Literature

## Nomination and award procedure
### Potential candidates
From the start the Nobel Prize in Literature attracted much media attention. The first prize in 1901 was reported in hundreds of newspapers in different parts of the world.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Tenngart-70) The prizes to Rudyard Kipling in 1907 and Rabindranath Tagore in 1913 helped to establish the prize as a central phenomenon in world literature. After World War II, the prize has earned more intense media attention with dramatic news reports and in-depth comments from around the world, further establishing its central position in the global literary space.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Tenngart-70) Days before the announcement of the year's Nobel laureate in Literature, potential winners are widely guessed in the media, and controversial and surprising choices have often caused much media discussion.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Tenngart-70)
Although the Nobel Prize in Literature is widely regarded as the world's most prestigious literary prize,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-71) the Swedish Academy has attracted significant criticism for its handling of the award.
Many authors who have won the prize have fallen into obscurity, while others rejected by the jury remain widely studied and read. In the _Wall Street Journal_, Joseph Epstein wrote, "You might not know it, but you and I are members of a club whose fellow members include Leo Tolstoy, Henry James, Anton Chekhov, Mark Twain, Henrik Ibsen, Marcel Proust, James Joyce, Jorge Luis Borges and Vladimir Nabokov. The club is the Non-Winners of the Nobel Prize in Literature. All these authentically great writers, still alive when the prize, initiated in 1901, was being awarded, didn't win it."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-72)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Potential candidates
Other notable names from the non-western canon who were ignored despite being nominated several times for the prize include Sri Aurobindo and Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan. The prize has "become widely seen as a political one – a peace prize in literary disguise", whose judges are prejudiced against authors with political tastes different from theirs.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-73)
Tim Parks has expressed skepticism that it is possible for "Swedish professors ... [to] compar[e] a poet from Indonesia, perhaps translated into English with a novelist from Cameroon, perhaps available only in French, and another who writes in Afrikaans but is published in German and Dutch...".[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-74)
As of 2021, 16 of the 118 recipients have been of Scandinavian origin. The Academy has often been alleged to be biased towards European, and in particular Swedish, authors.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-75)
Nobel's "vague" wording for the criteria for the prize has led to recurrent controversy. In the original Swedish, the word _idealisk_ translates as "ideal."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-swedishref-3)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Espmark2-76)
The Nobel Committee's interpretation has varied over the years. In recent years, this means a kind of idealism championing human rights on a broad scale.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-swedishref-3)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-NSmith-77)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Controversies about Nobel laureate selections
[edit]
From 1901 to 1912, the committee, led by the conservative Carl David af Wirsén, assessed the literary quality of a work in relation to its contribution to humanity's pursuit of the "ideal." Leo Tolstoy, Henrik Ibsen, Émile Zola, and Mark Twain were rejected in favour of authors who mostly are little read today.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Espmark2-76)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-78)
Later, the prize has often been controversial due to the Swedish Academy's Eurocentric choices of laureates, or for political reasons, as seen in the years 1970, 2005, and 2019, and for the Academy awarding its own members, as happened in 1974.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-79)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Nationality-based criticism
[edit]
French author Albert Camus was the first African-born writer to receive the award.
The prize's focus on European men, and Swedes in particular, has been the subject of criticism, even from Swedish newspapers.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-80) The majority of laureates have been European, with Sweden itself receiving more prizes (8) than all of Asia (7, if Turkish Orhan Pamuk is included), as well as all of Latin America (7, if Saint Lucian Derek Walcott is included). In 2009, Horace Engdahl, then the permanent secretary of the Academy, declared that "Europe still is the centre of the literary world" and that "the US is too isolated, too insular. They don't translate enough and don't really participate in the big dialogue of literature."[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-81)
In 2009, Engdahl's replacement, Peter Englund, rejected this sentiment ("In most language areas ... there are authors that really deserve and could get the Nobel Prize and that goes for the United States and the Americas, as well") and acknowledged the Eurocentric nature of the award, saying that, "I think that is a problem. We tend to relate more easily to literature written in Europe and in the European tradition."[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-82) American critics are known to object that those from their own country, like Philip Roth, Thomas Pynchon, and Cormac McCarthy, have been overlooked, as have Latin Americans such as Jorge Luis Borges, Julio Cortázar, and Carlos Fuentes, while in their place Europeans lesser-known to that continent have triumphed. The 2009 award to Herta Müller, previously little-known outside Germany but many times named favourite for the Nobel Prize, re-ignited the viewpoint that the Swedish Academy was biased and Eurocentric.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-83)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Nationality-based criticism
The 2010 prize was awarded to Mario Vargas Llosa, a native of Peru in South America, a generally well-regarded decision. When the 2011 prize was awarded to the Swedish poet Tomas Tranströmer, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy Peter Englund said the prize was not decided based on politics, describing such a notion as "literature for dummies."[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-84) The Swedish Academy awarded the next two prizes to non-Europeans, Chinese author Mo Yan and Canadian short story writer Alice Munro. French writer Patrick Modiano's win in 2014 renewed questions of Eurocentrism; when asked by _The Wall Street Journal_ "So no American this year, yet again. Why is that?", Englund reminded Americans of the Canadian origins of the previous year's recipient, the Academy's desire for literary quality and the impossibility of rewarding everyone who deserves the prize.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-no_american_again_this_year-85)

## Similar international prizes
[edit]
The Nobel Prize in Literature is not the only literary prize for which all nationalities are eligible. Other notable international literary prizes include the Neustadt International Prize for Literature, the Jerusalem Prize, Franz Kafka Prize, the International Booker Prize, and the Formentor Prix International. The journalist Hephzibah Anderson has noted that the International Booker Prize "is fast becoming the more significant award, appearing an ever more competent alternative to the Nobel".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-86) However, since 2016, the International Booker Prize now recognises an annual book of fiction translated into English.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-87) Previous winners of the International Booker Prize who have gone on to win the Nobel Prize in Literature include Alice Munro, Olga Tokarczuk, and Han Kang.
The Neustadt International Prize for Literature is regarded as one of the most prestigious international literary prizes, often referred to as the American equivalent of the Nobel Prize.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-88)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-89) Like the Nobel Prize, it is awarded not for any one work but for an entire body of work. It is frequently seen as an indicator of who may be awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature. Gabriel García Márquez (1972 Neustadt, 1982 Nobel), Czesław Miłosz (1978 Neustadt, 1980 Nobel), Octavio Paz (1982 Neustadt, 1990 Nobel), Tomas Tranströmer (1990 Neustadt, 2011 Nobel) were first awarded the Neustadt International Prize for Literature before being awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.

## Similar international prizes
Another award of note is the Spanish Princess of Asturias Award (formerly Prince of Asturias Award) in Letters. During the first years of its existence it was almost exclusively awarded to writers in the Spanish language, but in more recent times, writers in other languages have been awarded as well. Writers who have won both the Asturias Award in Letters and the Nobel Prize in Literature include Camilo José Cela, Günter Grass, Doris Lessing, and Mario Vargas Llosa.
The non-monetary America Award in Literature presents itself as an alternative to the Nobel Prize. Peter Handke, Harold Pinter, José Saramago, and Mario Vargas Llosa are the only writers to have received both the America Award and the Nobel Prize in Literature.
There are also prizes for honouring the lifetime achievement of writers in specific languages, like the Miguel de Cervantes Prize (for Spanish language, established in 1976) and the Camões Prize (for Portuguese language, established in 1989). Nobel laureates who were also awarded the Miguel de Cervantes Prize include Octavio Paz (1981 Cervantes, 1990 Nobel); Mario Vargas Llosa (1994 Cervantes, 2010 Nobel); and Camilo José Cela (1995 Cervantes, 1989 Nobel). José Saramago is the only author to receive both the Camões Prize (1995) and the Nobel Prize (1998) to date.
The Hans Christian Andersen Award is sometimes referred to as "the Little Nobel". The award has earned this appellation since, in a similar manner to the Nobel Prize in Literature, it recognises the lifetime achievement of writers, though the Andersen Award focuses on a single category of literary works (children's literature).[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-90)

The **Nobel Prize in Literature**, here meaning _for_ Literature (Swedish: _Nobelpriset i litteratur_), is a Swedish literature prize that is awarded annually to an author from any country who has, in the words of Alfred Nobel, "in the field of literature, produced the most outstanding work in an idealistic direction".[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelorglit-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-swedishref-3) Though individual works are sometimes cited as being particularly noteworthy, the award is based on an author's body of work as a whole. The Swedish Academy decides who, if anyone, will receive the prize.
The academy announces the name of the laureate in early October. It is one of the five Nobel Prizes established by the will of Alfred Nobel in 1895. Literature is traditionally the final award presented at the Nobel Prize ceremony. On some occasions, the award has been postponed to the following year, most recently in 2018.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelBBC-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-akademi2018-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-krisen-6)
texts.1:
In 1901, French poet and essayist Sully Prudhomme (1839–1907) was the first person to be awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, "in special recognition of his poetic composition, which gives evidence of lofty idealism, artistic perfection, and a rare combination of the qualities of both heart and intellect."
Hemingway's telegram in 1954 (The academy has alternately used _for_ Literature and _in_ Literature over the years, the latter becoming the norm today.)
texts.2: Alfred Nobel stipulated in his last will and testament that his money be used to create a series of prizes for those who confer the "greatest benefit on mankind" in physics, chemistry, peace, physiology or medicine, and literature.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-BBCHistory-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Britannica6-8) Although Nobel wrote several wills during his lifetime, the last was written a little over a year before he died, and it was signed at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris on 27 November 1895.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-10) Nobel bequeathed 94% of his total assets, 31 million Swedish _kronor_ (US$198 million, €176 million in 2016), to establish and endow the five Nobel Prizes.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Nobelwill-11) Due to the level of scepticism surrounding the will, it was not until 26 April 1897 that the Storting (Norwegian Parliament) approved it.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelprize1-12)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Levinovitz13-13) The executors of his will were Ragnar Sohlman and Rudolf Lilljequist, who formed the Nobel Foundation to take care of Nobel's fortune and organise the prizes.
texts.3: The members of the Norwegian Nobel Committee that were to award the Peace Prize were appointed shortly after the will was approved. The prize-awarding organisations followed: the Karolinska Institutet on 7 June, the Swedish Academy on 9 June, and the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences on 11 June.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-14)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-15) The Nobel Foundation then reached an agreement on guidelines for how the Nobel Prize should be awarded. In 1900, the Nobel Foundation's newly created statutes were promulgated by King Oscar II.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Levinovitz13-13)[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-thelocal1-16)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-BritannicaWill-17) According to Nobel's will, the prize in literature should be determined by "the Academy in Stockholm", which was specified by the statutes of the Nobel Foundation to mean the Swedish Academy.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Espmark-18)

## Nomination and award procedure
[edit]
Each year, the Swedish Academy sends out requests for nominations of candidates for the Nobel Prize in Literature. Members of the Academy, members of literature academies and societies, professors of literature and language, former Nobel literature laureates, and the presidents of writers' organisations are all allowed to nominate a candidate. One cannot nominate oneself.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobnoma-19)
Between 1901 and 1950, around 20 to 35 nominations were usually received each year.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-20) Since then, thousands of requests are sent out each year, and as of 2011 about 220 proposals were returned.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-wastberg-21) These proposals must be received by the Academy by 1 February, after which they are examined by the Nobel Committee, a working group within the Academy comprising four to five members.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobnomb-22) By April, the committee narrows the field to around 20 candidates.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-wastberg-21) By May, a shortlist of five names is approved by the Academy.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-wastberg-21) The next four months are spent reading and reviewing the works of the five candidates.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-wastberg-21) In October, members of the Academy vote, and the candidate who receives more than half of the votes is named the Nobel laureate in Literature.
texts.5:
## Nomination and award procedure
No one can get the prize without being on the shortlist at least twice; thus, many authors reappear and are reviewed repeatedly over the years.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-wastberg-21) The academicians read works in their original language, but when a candidate is shortlisted from a language that no member masters, they call on translators and oath-sworn experts to provide samples of that writer's work.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-wastberg-21) Other elements of the process are similar to those of other Nobel Prizes.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobnomb-22) The Swedish Academy is composed of 18 members who are elected for life and, until 2018, not technically permitted to leave.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-keyton-23) On 2 May 2018, King Carl XVI Gustaf amended the rules of the academy and made it possible for members to resign. The new rules also mention that a member who has been inactive in the work of the academy for more than two years can be asked to resign.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-DN-April-24)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-aftonbladetApril-25) The members of the Nobel committee are elected for a period of three years from among the members of the academy and are assisted by specially appointed expert advisers.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-26)
texts.6:
## Nomination and award procedure
The award is usually announced in October. Sometimes, however, the award has been announced the year after the nominal year, the latest such case being the 2018 award. In the midst of controversy surrounding claims of sexual assault, conflict of interest, and resignations by officials, on 4 May 2018, the Swedish Academy announced that the 2018 laureate would be announced in 2019 along with the 2019 laureate.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-akademi2018-5)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelBBC-4) Some years, such as in 1949, no candidate received the required majority of the votes, and for that reason, the prize was postponed and announced the following year.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-27)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Withdrawn, invalidated and unarchived nominations
[edit]
Between 1901 and 1970, literary historians and archivists noted that there were official nominees who were either withdrawn, invalidated or not archived in the Academy's nomination database.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-fact-28) In 1911, the Swedish playwright August Strindberg was nominated for the first time by Academy member Nathan Söderblom but because the nomination "arrived too late", it was withdrawn and unarchived unlike any other nominations that were moved to the succeeding year.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-fact-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-29) In 1904, José Echegaray's nomination letter "arrived late due to slow mail service" and Rudyard Kipling's had been temporarily misplaced. It was then decided by the Nobel committee to include both the nominations for 1904 and not moved for 1905.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-30)
texts.8:
## Nomination and award procedure
### Withdrawn, invalidated and unarchived nominations
There have been nine recorded occasions when the nominations were declared invalid. The only nominations for Pedro Pablo Figueroa, [Max Haushofer Jr.](https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max%20Haushofer%20Jr. "de:Max Haushofer Jr."), William Booth and Armando Alvares Pedroso were declared invalid by the Nobel committee because their respective nominators were found to be ineligible.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelpris-32) Such declarations also occurred to Ernest Lavisse in 1911, Henriette Charasson in 1945, Teixeira de Pascoaes in 1945 and Enrique Larreta in 1945._[why?_] Therefore, their names were withdrawn from the archives in those specific years.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelpris-32)John Macmillan Brown's self-nomination under the pseudonym "Godfrey Sweven" was declared invalid due to the rule that nominations of oneself is impermissible.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-33)
Permanent Secretary of the Swedish Academy Anders Österling revealed to the _New York Times_ days before the announcement that Willa Cather, together with Ernest Hemingway, John Steinbeck, and Gabriela Mistral, was among the contenders for the 1944 prize. *   **Highest number of nominees in a year**: 114 writers were nominated in 1975.  
*   **Highest number of new nominees in a year:** 30 new writers were nominated in 1969.

*   **Number of women**: 89

*   **Oldest female nominee**: At age 92, Estonian poet Marie Under was nominated in 1975.  
*   **Youngest male nominee**: At age 29, Icelandic writer Gunnar Gunnarsson was nominated in 1918.

A Literature Nobel Prize laureate receives a gold medal, a diploma bearing a citation, and a sum of money.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-50) The amount of money awarded depends on the income of the Nobel Foundation that year.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-nobelprize2-51)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Potential candidates
From the start the Nobel Prize in Literature attracted much media attention. The first prize in 1901 was reported in hundreds of newspapers in different parts of the world.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Tenngart-70) The prizes to Rudyard Kipling in 1907 and Rabindranath Tagore in 1913 helped to establish the prize as a central phenomenon in world literature. After World War II, the prize has earned more intense media attention with dramatic news reports and in-depth comments from around the world, further establishing its central position in the global literary space.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Tenngart-70) Days before the announcement of the year's Nobel laureate in Literature, potential winners are widely guessed in the media, and controversial and surprising choices have often caused much media discussion.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Tenngart-70)
Although the Nobel Prize in Literature is widely regarded as the world's most prestigious literary prize,[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-71) the Swedish Academy has attracted significant criticism for its handling of the award.
Many authors who have won the prize have fallen into obscurity, while others rejected by the jury remain widely studied and read. In the _Wall Street Journal_, Joseph Epstein wrote, "You might not know it, but you and I are members of a club whose fellow members include Leo Tolstoy, Henry James, Anton Chekhov, Mark Twain, Henrik Ibsen, Marcel Proust, James Joyce, Jorge Luis Borges and Vladimir Nabokov. The club is the Non-Winners of the Nobel Prize in Literature. All these authentically great writers, still alive when the prize, initiated in 1901, was being awarded, didn't win it."[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-72)

Other notable names from the non-western canon who were ignored despite being nominated several times for the prize include Sri Aurobindo and Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan. The prize has "become widely seen as a political one – a peace prize in literary disguise", whose judges are prejudiced against authors with political tastes different from theirs.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-73)
Tim Parks has expressed skepticism that it is possible for "Swedish professors ... [to] compar[e] a poet from Indonesia, perhaps translated into English with a novelist from Cameroon, perhaps available only in French, and another who writes in Afrikaans but is published in German and Dutch...".[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-74)
As of 2021, 16 of the 118 recipients have been of Scandinavian origin. The Academy has often been alleged to be biased towards European, and in particular Swedish, authors.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-75)
Nobel's "vague" wording for the criteria for the prize has led to recurrent controversy. In the original Swedish, the word _idealisk_ translates as "ideal."[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-swedishref-3)[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Espmark2-76)
The Nobel Committee's interpretation has varied over the years. In recent years, this means a kind of idealism championing human rights on a broad scale.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-swedishref-3)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-NSmith-77)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Controversies about Nobel laureate selections
[edit]
From 1901 to 1912, the committee, led by the conservative Carl David af Wirsén, assessed the literary quality of a work in relation to its contribution to humanity's pursuit of the "ideal." Leo Tolstoy, Henrik Ibsen, Émile Zola, and Mark Twain were rejected in favour of authors who mostly are little read today.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-Espmark2-76)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-78)
Later, the prize has often been controversial due to the Swedish Academy's Eurocentric choices of laureates, or for political reasons, as seen in the years 1970, 2005, and 2019, and for the Academy awarding its own members, as happened in 1974.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-79)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Nationality-based criticism
[edit]
French author Albert Camus was the first African-born writer to receive the award.
The prize's focus on European men, and Swedes in particular, has been the subject of criticism, even from Swedish newspapers.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-80) The majority of laureates have been European, with Sweden itself receiving more prizes (8) than all of Asia (7, if Turkish Orhan Pamuk is included), as well as all of Latin America (7, if Saint Lucian Derek Walcott is included). In 2009, Horace Engdahl, then the permanent secretary of the Academy, declared that "Europe still is the centre of the literary world" and that "the US is too isolated, too insular. They don't translate enough and don't really participate in the big dialogue of literature."[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-81)
In 2009, Engdahl's replacement, Peter Englund, rejected this sentiment ("In most language areas ... there are authors that really deserve and could get the Nobel Prize and that goes for the United States and the Americas, as well") and acknowledged the Eurocentric nature of the award, saying that, "I think that is a problem. We tend to relate more easily to literature written in Europe and in the European tradition."[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-82) American critics are known to object that those from their own country, like Philip Roth, Thomas Pynchon, and Cormac McCarthy, have been overlooked, as have Latin Americans such as Jorge Luis Borges, Julio Cortázar, and Carlos Fuentes, while in their place Europeans lesser-known to that continent have triumphed. The 2009 award to Herta Müller, previously little-known outside Germany but many times named favourite for the Nobel Prize, re-ignited the viewpoint that the Swedish Academy was biased and Eurocentric.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-83)

## Nomination and award procedure
### Nationality-based criticism
The 2010 prize was awarded to Mario Vargas Llosa, a native of Peru in South America, a generally well-regarded decision. When the 2011 prize was awarded to the Swedish poet Tomas Tranströmer, permanent secretary of the Swedish Academy Peter Englund said the prize was not decided based on politics, describing such a notion as "literature for dummies."[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-84) The Swedish Academy awarded the next two prizes to non-Europeans, Chinese author Mo Yan and Canadian short story writer Alice Munro. French writer Patrick Modiano's win in 2014 renewed questions of Eurocentrism; when asked by _The Wall Street Journal_ "So no American this year, yet again. Why is that?", Englund reminded Americans of the Canadian origins of the previous year's recipient, the Academy's desire for literary quality and the impossibility of rewarding everyone who deserves the prize.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-no_american_again_this_year-85)
texts.34:
## Similar international prizes
[edit]
The Nobel Prize in Literature is not the only literary prize for which all nationalities are eligible. Other notable international literary prizes include the Neustadt International Prize for Literature, the Jerusalem Prize, Franz Kafka Prize, the International Booker Prize, and the Formentor Prix International. The journalist Hephzibah Anderson has noted that the International Booker Prize "is fast becoming the more significant award, appearing an ever more competent alternative to the Nobel".[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-86) However, since 2016, the International Booker Prize now recognises an annual book of fiction translated into English.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-87) Previous winners of the International Booker Prize who have gone on to win the Nobel Prize in Literature include Alice Munro, Olga Tokarczuk, and Han Kang.
The Neustadt International Prize for Literature is regarded as one of the most prestigious international literary prizes, often referred to as the American equivalent of the Nobel Prize.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-88)[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-89) Like the Nobel Prize, it is awarded not for any one work but for an entire body of work. It is frequently seen as an indicator of who may be awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature. Gabriel García Márquez (1972 Neustadt, 1982 Nobel), Czesław Miłosz (1978 Neustadt, 1980 Nobel), Octavio Paz (1982 Neustadt, 1990 Nobel), Tomas Tranströmer (1990 Neustadt, 2011 Nobel) were first awarded the Neustadt International Prize for Literature before being awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature.
texts.35:
## Similar international prizes
Another award of note is the Spanish Princess of Asturias Award (formerly Prince of Asturias Award) in Letters. During the first years of its existence it was almost exclusively awarded to writers in the Spanish language, but in more recent times, writers in other languages have been awarded as well. Writers who have won both the Asturias Award in Letters and the Nobel Prize in Literature include Camilo José Cela, Günter Grass, Doris Lessing, and Mario Vargas Llosa.
The non-monetary America Award in Literature presents itself as an alternative to the Nobel Prize. Peter Handke, Harold Pinter, José Saramago, and Mario Vargas Llosa are the only writers to have received both the America Award and the Nobel Prize in Literature.
There are also prizes for honouring the lifetime achievement of writers in specific languages, like the Miguel de Cervantes Prize (for Spanish language, established in 1976) and the Camões Prize (for Portuguese language, established in 1989). Nobel laureates who were also awarded the Miguel de Cervantes Prize include Octavio Paz (1981 Cervantes, 1990 Nobel); Mario Vargas Llosa (1994 Cervantes, 2010 Nobel); and Camilo José Cela (1995 Cervantes, 1989 Nobel). José Saramago is the only author to receive both the Camões Prize (1995) and the Nobel Prize (1998) to date.
The Hans Christian Andersen Award is sometimes referred to as "the Little Nobel". The award has earned this appellation since, in a similar manner to the Nobel Prize in Literature, it recognises the lifetime achievement of writers, though the Andersen Award focuses on a single category of literary works (children's literature).[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Literature#cite_note-90)

The **Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine**[[a]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-2) is awarded yearly by the Nobel Assembly at the Karolinska Institute for outstanding discoveries in physiology or medicine. It is one of the five Nobel Prizes prizes that, in accordance with Alfred Nobel's 1895 will, are awarded "to those who, during the preceding year, have conferred the greatest benefit to humankind". Nobel Prizes are awarded in the fields of Physics, Medicine or Physiology, Chemistry, Literature, and Peace. A sixth prize, for Economic Sciences, was established in 1968 by Sveriges Riksbank (Sweden's central bank) in memory of Alfred Nobel.

The Nobel Prize is presented annually on the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death, 10 December. As of 2026, 117 Nobel Prizes in Physiology or Medicine have been awarded to 235 laureates, 221 men and 14 women. The first one was awarded in 1901 to the German physiologist, Emil von Behring, for his work on serum therapy and the development of a vaccine against diphtheria. The first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, Gerty Cori, received it in 1947 for her role in elucidating the metabolism of glucose, important in many aspects of medicine, including treatment of diabetes. The most recent Nobel prize was announced by the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institutet on 5 October 2026, and has been awarded to American Karl Deisseroth, Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, for their discoveries concerning light-gated ion channels and optogenetics.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-3)
The prize consists of a medal along with a diploma and a certificate for the monetary award. The front side of the medal displays the same profile of Alfred Nobel depicted on the medals for Physics, Chemistry, and Literature; the reverse side is unique to this medal.
Some awards have been controversial. This includes one to António Egas Moniz in 1949 for the prefrontal lobotomy, bestowed despite protests from the medical establishment. Other controversies resulted from disagreements over who was included in the award. The 1952 prize to Selman Waksman was litigated in court, and half the patent rights were awarded to his co-discoverer Albert Schatz who was not recognised by the prize. Nobel prizes cannot be awarded posthumously. Also, no more than three recipients can receive a Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, a limitation that is sometimes discussed because of an increasing trend for larger teams to conduct important scientific projects.
Nobel was interested in experimental physiology and set up his own laboratories.

Alfred Nobel was born on 21 October 1833 in Stockholm, Sweden, into a family of engineers.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Levinovitz5-4) He was a chemist, engineer and inventor who amassed a fortune during his lifetime, most of it from his 355 inventions, of which dynamite is the most famous.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Levinovitz11-5) He was interested in experimental physiology and set up his own labs in France and Italy to conduct experiments in blood transfusions. Keeping abreast of scientific findings, he was generous in his donations to Ivan Pavlov's laboratory in Russia and was optimistic about the progress resulting from scientific discoveries made in laboratories.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Feldman237-238-6)

In 1888, Nobel was surprised to read his own obituary, titled "The Merchant of death Is Dead", in a French newspaper. As it happened, it was Nobel's brother Ludvig who had died, but Nobel, unhappy with the content of the obituary and concerned that his legacy would reflect poorly on him, was inspired to change his will.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Time-7) In his last will, Nobel requested that his money be used to create a series of prizes for those who confer the "greatest benefit on mankind" in physics, chemistry, peace, physiology or medicine, and literature.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-BBCHistory-8) Though Nobel wrote several wills during his lifetime, the last was written a little over a year before he died in 1896 at the age of 63.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-9) Because his will was contested, it was not approved by the Storting (Norwegian Parliament) until 26 April 1897.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Levinovitz13-10)

After Nobel's death, the Nobel Foundation was set up to manage the assets of the bequest.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-nobelfoundation-11) In 1900, the Nobel Foundation's newly created statutes were promulgated by Swedish King Oscar II.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-thelocal1-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Levinovitz14-13) According to Nobel's will, the Karolinska Institute in Sweden, a medical school and research centre, is responsible for the Prize in Physiology or Medicine.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-14) Today, the prize is commonly referred to as the Nobel Prize in Medicine.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Levinovitz112-15)

## Nomination and selection
[edit]
The reverse side of the Nobel Prize for Physiology or Medicine
It was important to Nobel that the prize be awarded for a "discovery" and that it be of "greatest benefit on mankind".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Lindsten-16) Per the provisions of the will, only select persons are eligible to nominate individuals for the award. These include members of academies around the world, professors of medicine in Sweden, Denmark, Norway, Iceland, and Finland, as well as professors of selected universities and research institutions in other countries. Past Nobel laureates may also nominate.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-17) Until 1977, all professors of Karolinska Institute together decided on the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. That year, changes in Swedish law forced the institute to make public any documents pertaining to the Nobel Prize, and it was considered necessary to establish a legally independent body for the Prize work. Therefore, the Nobel Assembly was constituted, consisting of 50 professors at Karolinska Institute. It elects the Nobel Committee with five members who evaluate the nominees, the Secretary who is in charge of the organisation, and each year ten adjunct members to assist in the evaluation of candidates. In 1968, a provision was added that no more than three persons may share a Nobel prize.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Levinovitz17-18)

## Nomination and selection
True to its mandate, the committee has chosen researchers working in the basic sciences over those who have made applied science contributions. Harvey Cushing, a pioneering American neurosurgeon who identified [Cushing's syndrome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cushing's_syndrome "Cushing's syndrome"), was not awarded the prize, nor was Sigmund Freud, as his psychoanalysis lacks hypotheses that can be experimentally confirmed.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Feldman238-19) The public expected Jonas Salk or Albert Sabin to receive the prize for their development of the polio vaccines, but instead the award went to John Enders, Thomas Weller, and Frederick Robbins whose basic discovery that the polio virus could reproduce in monkey cells in laboratory preparations made the vaccines possible.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-bishop-20)
Through the 1930s, there were frequent prize laureates in classical physiology, but after that, the field began fragmenting into specialities. The last classical physiology laureates were John Eccles, Alan Hodgkin, and Andrew Huxley in 1963 for their findings regarding "unitary electrical events in the central and peripheral nervous system."[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Feldman239-21)
A Medicine or Physiology Nobel Prize laureate earns a gold medal, a diploma bearing a citation, and a sum of money.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-22) These are awarded during the prize ceremony at the Stockholm Concert Hall.
Alexander Fleming's 1945 Nobel Prize medal for Physiology or Medicine on display at the National Museum of Scotland, Edinburgh.

## Nomination and selection
The Physiology or Medicine medal has a portrait of Alfred Nobel in left profile on the obverse.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-NobelUnique-23) The medal was designed by Erik Lindberg.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-NobelUnique-23) The reverse of the medal depicts the 'Genius of Medicine holding an open book in her lap, collecting the water pouring out from a rock in order to quench a sick girl's thirst'.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-NobelMedicine-24) It is inscribed "_Inventas vitam iuvat excoluisse per artes_" ("It is beneficial to have improved (human) life through discovered arts") an adaptation of "_inventas aut qui vitam excoluere per artes_" from line 663 from book 6 of the _Aeneid_ by the Roman poet Virgil.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-NobelMedicine-24) A plate below the figures is inscribed with the name of the recipient. The text "REG. UNIVERSITAS MED. CHIR. CAROL." denoting the Karolinska Institute is also inscribed on the reverse.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-NobelMedicine-24)
Between 1902 and 2010 the Nobel Prize medals were struck by the Myntverket, the Swedish royal mint, located in Eskilstuna. In 2011 the medals were made by the Det Norske Myntverket in Kongsberg. The medals have been made by Svenska Medalj in Eskilstuna since 2012.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-NobelUnique-23)

## Nomination and selection
Nobel laureates receive a diploma directly from the King of Sweden. Each diploma is uniquely designed by the prize-awarding institutions for the laureate who receives it. In the case of the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, that is the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institute. Well-known artists and calligraphers from Sweden are commissioned to create it.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-nobelprize5-25) The diploma contains a picture and text which states the name of the laureate and a citation as to why they received the prize.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-nobelprize5-25)
At the awards ceremony, the laureate is given a document indicating the award sum. The amount of the cash award may differ from year to year, based on the funding available from the Nobel Foundation. For example, in 2009 the total cash awarded was 10 million SEK (US$1.4 million),[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-nobelprize2-26) but in 2012, the amount was 8 million Swedish Krona, or US$1.1 million.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-27) If there are two laureates in a particular category, the award grant is divided equally between the recipients, but if there are three, the awarding committee may opt to divide the grant equally, or award half to one recipient and a quarter to each of the two others.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-28)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-29)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-30)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-31)

## Nomination and selection
### Ceremony and banquet
[edit]
The awards are bestowed at a gala ceremony followed by a banquet.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-local-32) The Nobel Banquet is an extravagant affair with the menu, planned months ahead of time, kept secret until the day of the event. The Nobel Foundation chooses the menu after tasting and testing selections submitted by selected chefs of international repute. Currently, it is a three-course dinner, although it was originally six courses in 1901. Each Nobel Prize laureate may bring up to 16 guests. Sweden's royal family attends, and typically the Prime Minister and other members of the government attend as well as representatives of the Nobel family.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-33)
Emil von Behring received the first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1901.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Feldman242-34)

## Nomination and selection
### Ceremony and banquet
The first Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine was awarded in 1901 to the German physiologist Emil Adolf von Behring.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Feldman242-34) Behring's discovery of serum therapy in the development of the diphtheria and tetanus vaccines put "in the hands of the physician a victorious weapon against illness and deaths".[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-35)[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Behring-36) In 1902, the award went to Ronald Ross for his work on malaria, "by which he has shown how it enters the organism and thereby has laid the foundation for successful research on this disease and methods of combating it".[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-37) He identified the mosquito as the transmitter of malaria, and worked tirelessly on measures to prevent malaria worldwide.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-38)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-39) The 1903 prize was awarded to Niels Ryberg Finsen, the first Faroese laureate, "in recognition of his contribution to the treatment of diseases, especially lupus vulgaris, with concentrated light radiation, whereby he has opened a new avenue for medical science".[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-40)[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-41) He died within a year after receiving the prize at the age of 43.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-finsen-42)Ivan Pavlov, whose work Nobel admired and supported,

## Nomination and selection
### Ceremony and banquet

Nikolaas Tinbergen (left) and Konrad Lorenz (right) were awarded (with Karl von Frisch) for their discoveries concerning animal behaviour.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-nobel-1973-44)
Subsequently, those selecting the recipients have exercised wide latitude in determining what falls under the umbrella of Physiology or Medicine. The awarding of the prize in 1973 to Nikolaas Tinbergen, Konrad Lorenz, and Karl von Frisch for their observations of animal behavioural patterns could be considered a prize in the behavioural sciences rather than medicine or physiology.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Levinovitz112-15) Tinbergen expressed surprise in his Nobel Prize acceptance speech at "the unconventional decision of the Nobel Foundation to award this year's prize 'for Physiology or Medicine' to three men who had until recently been regarded as 'mere animal watchers'".[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Tinbergen-45)
In 1947, Gerty Cori was the first woman to be awarded the Prize in Physiology or Medicine.

## Nomination and selection
### Ceremony and banquet
Laureates have been awarded the Nobel Prize in a wide range of fields that relate to physiology or medicine. Prizes have recognized significant discoveries in areas as diverse as signal transduction through G proteins, neurobiology, and intermediary metabolism. As of 2025, a total of 116 Nobel Prizes in Physiology or Medicine have been awarded to 232 individuals since 1901.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-nervesignaling-46)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-47)[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-48)
Thirteen women have received the prize: Gerty Cori (1947), Rosalyn Yalow (1977), Barbara McClintock (1983), Rita Levi-Montalcini (1986), Gertrude B. Elion (1988), Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard (1995), Linda B. Buck (2004), Françoise Barré-Sinoussi (2008), Elizabeth H. Blackburn (2009), Carol W. Greider (2009), May-Britt Moser (2014), Tu Youyou (2015), Katalin Karikó (2023) and Mary E. Brunkow (2025).[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-49) Only one woman, Barbara McClintock, has received an unshared prize in this category, for the discovery of genetic transposition.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-factsmedprize-50)[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-McClintock-51)

## Nomination and selection
### Ceremony and banquet
Mario Capecchi, Martin Evans, and Oliver Smithies were awarded the prize in 2007 for the discovery of a gene targeting procedure (a type of genetic recombination) for introducing homologous recombination in mice, employing embryonic stem cells through the development of the knockout mouse.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-52)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Hansson-53) In 2009, the Nobel Prize was awarded to Elizabeth Blackburn, Carol W. Greider and Jack W. Szostak of the United States for discovering the process by which chromosomes are protected by telomeres (regions of repetitive DNA at the ends of chromosomes) and the enzyme telomerase.[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Wade-54)
Rita Levi-Montalcini, an Italian neurologist, who together with colleague Stanley Cohen and Lucas Pu, received the 1986 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for their discovery of nerve growth factor (NGF), was the first Nobel laureate to reach the 100th birthday.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-prizefacts-55)
Through 2025, the prize has been awarded to a single individual 40 times, shared by two laureates 35 times, and shared by three laureates 41 times (the maximum allowed).

## Nomination and selection
### Time factor and death
[edit]
Ralph M. Steinman was an inadvertent posthumous recipient of the Prize.
Because of the length of time that may pass before the significance of a discovery becomes apparent, some prizes are awarded many years after the initial discovery. Barbara McClintock made her discoveries in 1944, before the structure of the DNA molecule was known; she was not awarded the prize until 1983. Similarly, in 1916 Peyton Rous discovered the role of tumour viruses in chickens, but was not awarded the prize until 50 years later, in 1966.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Levinovitz114-56)Nobel laureate Carol Greider's research leading to the prize was conducted over 20 years before. She noted that the passage of time is an advantage in the medical sciences, as it may take many years for the significance of a discovery to become apparent.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Dreifus-57)
In 2011, Canadian immunologist Ralph M. Steinman was awarded the prize; however, unbeknownst to the committee, he had died three days before the announcement. The committee decided that since the prize was awarded "in good faith," it would be allowed to stand.

## Nomination and selection
### Controversial inclusions and exclusions
[edit]
Some of the awards have been controversial. The person who was deserving of the 1923 prize for the discovery of insulin as a central hormone for controlling diabetes (awarded only a year after its discovery)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Judson291-58) has been heatedly debated. It was shared between Frederick Banting and John Macleod; this infuriated Banting who regarded Macleod's involvement as minimal. Macleod was the department head at the University of Toronto but otherwise was not directly involved in the findings. Banting thought his laboratory partner Charles Best, who had shared in the laboratory work of discovery, should have shared the prize with him as well. In fairness, he decided to give half of his prize money to Best. Macleod on his part felt the biochemist James Collip, who joined the laboratory team later, deserved to be included in the award and shared his prize money with him.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-Judson291-58) Some maintain that Nicolae Paulescu, a Romanian professor of physiology at the University of Medicine and Pharmacy in Bucharest, was the first to isolate insulin, in 1916, although his pancrein was an impure aqueous extract unfit for human treatment similar to the one used previously by Israel Kleiner.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-J._Nutrition_92-59)[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-nrjs-60)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-nrps-61) When Banting published the paper that brought him the Nobel,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nobel_Prize_in_Physiology_or_Medicine#cite_note-nrks-62) Paulescu already held a patent for his discovery (10 April 1922, patent no.

## Nomination and selection
### Controversial inclusions and exclusions
